options.label: The StringBuilder that `a` used to refer to
options.feedback: Yes. Nothing refers to it any more: `a` was set to null and no other variable or field points to it.

options.label: The String `b`
options.feedback: Not yet — it is reachable from the static field `keep`, a GC root, and from the local `b`.

options.label: The list `keep`
options.feedback: Not yet — static fields are roots; the list stays alive as long as its class is loaded.

hints: For each object, look for a chain of references from a root: a live local variable or a static field.
exercises.solution: **a**. After `a = null`, no local, field or other object refers to the StringBuilder, so it is unreachable and may be collected. The string `b` is reachable from the static list `keep` (and from the local `b`), and `keep` itself is a static field. Note that "may be" is the right phrase: the collector reclaims unreachable objects whenever it next runs, not immediately.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson's GC log, young collections reduced the heap from 85M to 3M in under a millisecond. What best explains why they were so fast?

options.label: A young collection copies only the surviving objects, and almost nothing survived
options.feedback: Yes. Its cost is proportional to the live objects, not to the garbage.

options.label: The collector visits each dead object and frees it individually, and byte arrays are easy to free
options.feedback: Not yet — copying collectors never visit dead objects at all; the space they occupied is simply reused.

options.label: The collector skipped the work because System.gc() had already cleaned the heap
options.feedback: Not yet — each young collection really reclaimed about 80 MB of new garbage.

hints: What does a young collection have to do with a dead object? And with a live one?
exercises.solution: **a**. Young collections in G1 are copying collections: the collector traces from the roots, copies reachable young objects to a survivor or old region, and treats the rest of the young regions as free. Dead objects are never touched, so 80 MB of scratch arrays cost nothing to reclaim. This is the generational hypothesis paying off.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson, the Collatz search took 0.79 s with the JIT and 15.07 s with `-Xint` (interpreter only). To the nearest whole number, how many times faster was the JIT-compiled run?

feedback.message: Not yet — divide the interpreted time by the JIT time.

exercises.solution: 15.07 ÷ 0.79 ≈ 19.1, so about **19** times faster. The exact factor depends on the program and machine, but an order of magnitude or more for hot, numeric loops is typical: the interpreter executes each bytecode with a dispatch step, while C2 turns the loop into a few tight machine instructions.

exercises.prompt: A method calls itself with no base case. Which `Throwable` subclass does the JVM eventually throw? Give its simple class name.

feedback.message: Not yet — the frames live on the thread's stack, not on the heap. Which area runs out?
Nearly — Java names it an Error, not an Exception.

hints: Each call pushes a frame onto the thread's stack, which has a fixed size.
exercises.solution: **`StackOverflowError`**. Each call adds a frame to the thread's stack, which is of fixed size, and when it is full the JVM throws `StackOverflowError`. It is an `Error`, signalling a condition applications should not normally try to handle; the fix is a base case, or turning deep recursion into a loop.

exercises.prompt: A colleague times a method by calling it 1,000 times in a loop with `System.nanoTime()` around the loop, discarding the results. Which problems may make the measurement misleading? Choose all that apply.

options.label: Early calls run in the interpreter or C1 code, so the timing includes warm-up
options.feedback: Yes. Steady-state performance appears only after C2 has compiled the hot code.

options.label: Because the results are discarded, the JIT may eliminate the computation entirely
options.feedback: Yes. Dead-code elimination can turn the benchmark into an empty loop.

options.label: A GC pause or another process may land inside the timed region
options.feedback: Yes. Single measurements are noisy; you need repetitions and statistics.

options.label: `System.nanoTime()` only has a resolution of whole seconds
options.feedback: Not yet — nanoTime is a high-resolution timer. The problems lie in what is being timed.

hints: Think about what the JIT does in the first moments, and what it may do to code whose results nobody uses.
exercises.solution: **a**, **b** and **c**. Warm-up, dead-code elimination and noise are the classic traps; others include constant folding and unrealistic type profiles. JMH addresses them by running warm-up iterations, forking fresh JVMs, consuming results through a "blackhole" and reporting averages with error bounds.

exercises.prompt: A trading service with a 48 GB heap must keep every request under 5 ms, and pause times from G1 are breaking that budget. Which collector is the natural thing to try first?

options.label: ZGC (`-XX:+UseZGC`)
options.feedback: Yes. ZGC does almost all its work concurrently and keeps pauses well under a millisecond, even with large heaps.

options.label: Parallel (`-XX:+UseParallelGC`)
options.feedback: Not yet — Parallel maximises throughput but stops the world for every collection; with a 48 GB heap its pauses would be long.

options.label: Serial (`-XX:+UseSerialGC`)
options.feedback: Not yet — a single-threaded stop-the-world collector on a 48 GB heap would pause for a long time.

options.label: None: call `System.gc()` every second so collections stay small
options.feedback: Not yet — System.gc() typically triggers full, stop-the-world collections, the slowest kind.

hints: The requirement is about pause length, not total throughput.
exercises.solution: **ZGC**. It is designed for low latency at any heap size, doing marking, relocation and reference fixing concurrently with the application, at some cost in throughput and memory. As always, turn on GC logging and measure before and after: the right collector is the one that meets the service's real requirements.
